pages.title: Polite requests

head: Pattern
Example
rows: Can I have a cake, please?

rules: Please goes at the end (or beginning): Coffee, please. / Please, coffee.
Can I have…? is polite. I want… can sound rude.
Thanks is informal; Thank you is neutral; Thank you very much is strong.
Say Excuse me BEFORE you speak or pass; say Sorry AFTER a mistake.
examples: Can I have some water, please?
Excuse me, where is the bakery?
Com licença, onde fica a padaria?

pages.title: Polite intonation
pages.tip: Polite English goes UP and DOWN. In a request, your voice rises on 'please' and then falls. A flat voice sounds rude! Listen to the difference.

pages.head: Politeness is free
text: Omar's bakery on Maple Street opens at six. At seven there is a long line outside. Everybody is polite. A woman says, "Good morning! A coffee and a bread roll, please." Omar answers, "Here you are." "Thank you very much!" "You're welcome!"
A boy bumps into a man in the line. "Oh, sorry!" says the boy. "No problem," says the man. A girl wants to pass: "Excuse me, please." Everybody makes space.
Omar smiles. "Polite words are free," he says, "but they make everybody happy." On the wall there is a sign: PLEASE and THANK YOU are always welcome here.
tf: The boy says 'Excuse me' when he bumps into the man.
qs: A coffee and a bread roll
Please and thank you are welcome
pages.talk: What polite words do you hear most in your country?

pages.title: Politeness: fact file

facts.label: the most British word
facts.sub: Brits say it even when it is not their fault

text: In English-speaking countries, people say 'please' and 'thank you' all the time, even to bus drivers and shop assistants.
In the UK, 'sorry' can mean 'excuse me', 'pardon?' or 'I disagree'. Listen to the tone!
In the USA, servers often say 'You're welcome' or 'My pleasure' after 'Thank you'.
